title: Bedlam’s “Othello” is running through May 31st at the West End Theatr...
transcript: not only is this production of Shakespeare's Othello performed with only four actors playing all the roles it's also kind of like fan service for long time followers of this acclaimed theatre company. the staging is fairly bare bones but there are moments where the direction really popped either with the use of space around the theatre or with the strong focus on a physical intimacy between the characters which permeates a lot of this production. and some fun little flashes of modern imagery like Cassio singing karaoke while he's drunk or Othello and Iago drinking beers together which is like a pretty simple choice but it evokes that quintessential image of disarmed masculine bonding that makes Iago's manipulations feel all the more believable what really sets it apart though is the all around phenomenal acting: not just the skillful switching between characters but the focused vulnerable and emotionally rich portrayals of each character individually and I guess that's no surprise because for Bedlam Theatre this company is a bit of an all star cast, led by some of their core members in a bit of a return to their roots. the context here is that about 14 years ago Bedlam started making waves in the New York theatre scene with its scrappy DIY productions of classics like Hamlet and Saint John with only four actors. since then though they've become a pretty well established presence doing somewhat more traditional work and casting a wider net of new faces alongside their regulars. so this Othello sort of feels like the MCU bringing back the old Spider Men or casting Robert Downey Jr in a new role like it is very fun and exciting but also as a long time fan of Bedlam I do think their creative vision has been a bit scattered and inconsistent recently so it does make me wonder what a return to form like this indicates about their creative direction moving forward. it also invites more scrutiny onto the thing itself because while Bedlam is still a small company in many ways there's no pretending that this four-actor setup is being done out of necessity so you're more inclined to ask what is it bringing to the table artistically? and there are some exciting theatrical beats that come out of their use of the four actor format here but mostly it felt like a fairly straightforward production of Othello just kind of happened to have four actors and pretty sparse staging: sometimes it adds a little sometimes it detracts a little but it doesn't do a whole lot of either in terms of presenting a distinct and angle or take on this play. having said that I still enjoyed it a lot more than not. It helps that this, is of course, a remarkably good, emotionally devastating play and that I haven't seen it in like seven years so I was revisiting it with comparatively fresh eyes. and it's possible that, without that, I wouldn't have had as much patience for the production. maybe I would have wanted it to amount to more than just an impressive acting showcase but as it stands I was still pretty happy to be a spectator for their well earned flexing
reasoning: Reviewer praises the acting as phenomenal and enjoyed it more than not, but has real reservations about whether the four-actor format brings much artistically and admits fresh eyes helped his patience.
keyQuote: I was still pretty happy to be a spectator for their well earned flexing
